title: The magnetic compass
summary: The Chinese long knew that a magnetic needle points north-south, and by the eleventh century they had turned their south pointer into a magnetic compass. In Song times the needle was made smaller and fixed to a stem, sometimes in a small case with a glass top, which suited it to sea travel. The first reports of such use date to 1119. The first definite European account, by Alexander Neckam, dates from about 1187, and the compass also reached the Islamic world.

as_recorded.value: The first reports of a compass used in this way date to 1119.
By the eleventh century a.d., the Chinese had turned their south pointer into a magnetic compass, and a century later this device spread to both Europe and the Islamic world.
